questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to a European English-speaking country, where there would be an option to study EU law in different aspects. Moreover, the possibility to enhance my English made me choose Dublin as my first priority. Also, I had never been to Ireland before, so I saw it as a good opportunity to visit the country and explore its beautiful nature more in-depth.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was overall the best semester of my education. So much fun living in a new city, meeting new people and getting friends for a lifetime, and also Dublin is great, and so are Ireland and the Irish people.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was alright. It just takes some time in general. You need to be prepared for using some time to look into different stuff. Mostly accommodation, which neither Københavns Universitet nor Trinity College can help with. However, you should not be scared away by this, because once you have been appointed a university the university's contact persons are very helpful and a lot of information will be given in due time. For me, I wanted to know everything as soon as possible, but it comes along as time goes.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got some assistance from my accommodation and also from Trinity College and our contact person. However, the orientation week was a bit disappointing. It seemed very unprepared and the students were not that great at preparing you for the semester, so for a long time, I was a bit unsure about how Trinity worked. Also, the introduction week was not very filled up, so two or three days there was only something scheduled for an hour, which makes the rest of the day available. When starting a new place, not knowing anybody, it could have been nice if something more had been prepared.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was very lucky to accidentally write myself up on a waiting list for Kavanaugh Court (student accommodation) as soon as I got the news that I was going to Trinity College. Kavanaugh Court is about 15 min walking distance from Trinity College and at the centre of Dublin (it is in Dublin one), so very easy to get around, also because the Luas (sporvogn) is just 5 min away. Kavanaugh works with Trinity, but you don't feel that when living there besides most students studying at Trinity. It was very nice compared to what others had found. In general, it is very hard to find accommodation. I would recommend starting looking as soon as you know you have been assigned Dublin as your destination.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is very common to live off campus in Dublin. Most do that. But when living in a student accommodation you can talk to other people in your hallway. In my hallway we were 7 people sharing a kitchen (had own bathroom), so there you got the sense and connection to college.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is hard and expensive to find and live in Dublin. More than Copenhagen. My stay at Kavanaugh Court costs around 5000 euro.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You are sent a link where you sign up for the courses you want. It is divided into categories regarding timetables, so you have no time clashes. However, it is possible to switch class if you change your mind when you arrive.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The Erasmus contact person was helpful. Otherwise, I used these travel reports for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
Very. I got my first priorities. I studied Environmental Law, Intellectual Property Law, and Eu Competition Law. 
However, I do not recommend EU Competition law, the professor is not that good. He cancelled most of our classes and the way he taught was ridiculous. He just read from a book. No PowerPoint, or interaction.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Choose what interests you and what kind of exams there are. It can be an advantage to take those classes where there are essays as exam type. All exams are usually in one week in December, so you can have two exams in one day (one of the Swedish Erasmus students experienced this, with only 1-hour break between the two). Therefore those courses with essays make that week easier. Also for the first and second-year courses, the exams are usually in an exam hall with thousands of other students and you have to write your exam in hand. I did not experience this, but some of the other Danes did, and it did not sound nice. 
All my courses were third and fourth-year courses, and the school burden was not overwhelming so you shouldn't be discouraged by that.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Not that impressed. It is not as hard as at Københavns Universitet.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had third and fourth-year level courses, and found them to be pretty easy. It is mostly difficult to find the right level on studying. In environmental law it was not expected that you read that much, but then it was a good idea to come to classes and pay attention. In Intellectual Property law there was a book, which I recommend reading (in part). There will be a new teacher in that module for next year, but the last one expected us to read for class. In Eu Competition Law there wasn't that much expectations, but the teacher was sooo bad, so hopefully they replace him.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: A monologue from the teachers. No presentations or group/casework. There was a group exam in Environmental law, but that was optional and could be made individually. I choose to stay in a group, it felt a little bit safer having an Irish student to help with the general stuff.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
EU Competition law
Environmental law
Intellectual Property Law

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There will be made some changes due to new teachers. Especially Intellectual property law, where there will come a new teacher. But this class is interesting. Also Environmental law, where the teacher is very ambitious and you learn a lot. However, the international community is very big at Trinity also among the teachers and two of my teachers were not from Ireland, but from India and Italy, so there were some thick accents to comprehend.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I spent a lot more on eating out and going to pubs. We did that a lot. Also travelling across Ireland was quite expensive in total, not much individually. Therefore the monthly budget for food is quite high.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and drinks are less expensive, but you just go out more, so it kinda equals up.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are so many clubs and social societies to join. I joined the Knitting Club, the Food and Drinks club, the Hiking club etc. I joined many but didn't use them all, because there are so many activities all the time. I had planned to do a lot with the hiking club, but went often with some of the other Erasmus students on our own.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Basket ball club, running club, knitting club, german club, irish club etc. There are over 120 clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a club! Maybe one and then do that more intensely if you want to expand your friend group. Otherwise, join a lot of different and go with your friends. The numbers of tickets for the different events are limited, so be ready to buy when tickets are made available!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore Ireland! There is so much to see and do, and it is so beautiful! I recommend taking a longer bus trip to see more. I visited Galway and Cliffs of Moher, Connemara, Ring of Kerry, Cork, Belfast and Giants Causeway (a 1-day bus trip from Belfast), Kilkenny etc. There are pretty good connections with bus and train around the country.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Yes pretty easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join and attend a lot in the beginning. A lot of your connections throughout the semester are made in the beginning. We were 4 Danes at Trinity and we became a very close group and hung out with a big group of Swedish but also a mixed group of German and French students. The most thing I would have wanted more was to have gotten more in contact with the Irish students, but somehow it seemed a bit difficult. But there are also so many international students (I think 24 % of Trinity students are international students). I got an Irish buddy (who can help with different stuff) and that was nice. We hung out sometimes and in groups with other Irish and Erasmus students as well.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The more laid back it was at Trinity. Otherwise, I didn't find that bid a cultural change.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The pubculture and the outgoing way Irish people in general are. They are welcoming.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Save money for accommodation, prepare yourself for exploring Ireland and Dublin (visit the Cathedral, Guinness Storehouse, Christ Church, Teeling distillery etc. there is so much to see and do) and be patient with Trinity College.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I arrived a week before school started to explore Ireland. I had booked a three day trip around Ireland by bus with a guide, and I can really recommend that. You get to see so much before school starts and therefore get the opportunity to travel a bit further away than what would be possible over the weekend. However, It is also possible to travel during the weekdays if you don't have school or can skip a lecture, or else there is the reading week in October, where I took a trip to Cork with some of the other Erasmus students.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friends I made and the experiences I had when visiting places in Ireland.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To maintain in contact with friends at home, because there was so much happening in Dublin with you friends there.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
